summary.text: The Hadean is the eon of Earth's history right after the planet formed, named after Hades, Greek god of the underworld, because its surface is thought to have been molten lava.
Its early air was thick with water vapor, methane and ammonia, but as the surface cooled, water condensed into a superocean that covered nearly the whole planet.
Hadean rocks are very rare and consist largely of zircon grains from one spot, the Jack Hills in Western Australia.

facts.label: Name origin
facts.value: Hades, Greek god of the underworld

items.prompt: Early Hadean Earth had a surface temperature around 230 °C, yet oceans of liquid water may have existed. How?

options.label: Dissolved salt stopped evaporation
Ice on top shielded the water
Very high air pressure kept it liquid
Young planets have no boiling point

items.explain: At an atmospheric pressure of about 27 atmospheres, water stays liquid even at such high temperatures.

items.prompt: Why did geologists name this eon after Hades, god of the underworld?

options.label: Its rocks lie deepest underground
Its surface was likely hellish lava
It ended in total darkness
Its fossils were found in caves

items.explain: The name refers to the hellish conditions on the newly formed Earth, whose surface is thought to have been molten.

items.prompt: Comet water has isotope ratios that don't match Earth's. So where did most of the water in the Hadean ocean most likely come from?

options.label: Icy comets striking Earth
Water carried in on the solar wind
Ice drifting in from Saturn's rings
Gas released from Earth's mantle

items.explain: Outgassing from the mantle is the most likely source; a large comet contribution is unlikely because the isotopes don't match.

items.prompt: Imagine an asteroid 100 kilometres across smashing into a Hadean ocean that covers the globe. What could it do?

options.label: Boil off up to 100 metres of ocean
Freeze the whole ocean solid
Leave the ocean completely unchanged
Knock Earth out of its orbit

items.explain: Each such impact could boil away up to 100 metres of a global ocean and briefly heat the air to 500 °C.

items.prompt: Why is direct evidence about Hadean geology from zircons considered limited?

options.label: Zircons cannot be dated reliably
Zircons dissolve quickly in water
Nearly all come from one place
They are all under a billion years old

items.explain: The zircons are largely gathered in a single locality in Australia, which narrows what they can tell us.

items.prompt: Hadean mantle rock likely churned more vigorously than today's. What made it flow so easily?

options.label: Ocean waves pushing on the crust
Radioactive heat and trapped water
Earth spinning much more slowly
Colder, stiffer rock cracking apart

items.explain: High radiogenic heat and water not yet outgassed lowered the mantle's viscosity, so convection was vigorous.
